What is FIP, and how is GS-441524 given?

A plain-language guide for cat owners facing a feline infectious peritonitis diagnosis: what the disease is, how treatment usually works, and how to make daily doses easier on you and your cat.

Reviewed by Ian Tasman, PharmD, owner and pharmacist · Updated November 18, 2026

What is FIP?

Feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) is a disease caused by a feline coronavirus. Many cats carry a mild form of this virus without getting sick. In a small number of cats, the virus changes inside the body and triggers a severe inflammatory disease. That's FIP.

FIP is seen most often in young cats, especially those under two years old, and in homes or shelters with several cats. It isn't the same as the coronavirus that causes COVID-19 in people.

The different forms

  • Wet (effusive) FIP: fluid builds up in the belly or chest, which can make the belly swell or breathing hard.
  • Dry (non-effusive) FIP: inflammation affects organs without much fluid. Signs can be vague, like fever, weight loss and low energy.
  • Eye or neurologic FIP: the disease reaches the eyes or brain, causing changes in the eyes, wobbliness, seizures or behavior changes.

Diagnosing FIP can be tricky, and your veterinarian puts together the history, exam, bloodwork and sometimes fluid testing to decide.

What is GS-441524?

For a long time, FIP was almost always fatal. GS-441524 is an antiviral that stops the virus from copying itself, and it has changed the outlook for many cats. It is not an FDA-approved drug. We compound it only from a veterinarian's prescription for a specific cat diagnosed with FIP, following FDA's published policy.

How treatment usually works

  • Daily doses for many weeks. Treatment commonly lasts at least 12 weeks (84 days), given every day. Your veterinarian sets the length.
  • The dose is based on weight. The amount depends on your cat's weight and the form of FIP, and it goes up as your cat gains weight. Weigh your cat weekly, ideally on a baby or kitchen scale, and send the weights to your vet.
  • Regular checkups. Your vet will recheck bloodwork during and after treatment to see how your cat is responding.
  • Don't stop early. Many cats look much better within days or weeks, but stopping before your vet says to can let the disease come back.

Giving GS-441524 at home

GS-441524 can be given by injection or by mouth. Many owners find oral medicine easier than daily injections. We prepare it as a flavored oral suspension in tuna, chicken or beef, measured with an oral syringe.

  1. Same time every day. Pick a time you can stick to, and set a phone reminder.
  2. Follow the food directions on your label. Your vet or pharmacist will tell you whether to give it with food or on an empty stomach.
  3. Use the oral syringe technique: slide the syringe into the cheek pouch behind the canine tooth, keep the head level and give it slowly. See our step-by-step guide.
  4. Keep a log. Write down each dose, your cat's weekly weight, appetite and energy. It helps your vet and helps you notice changes.
Call your veterinarian right away if your cat stops eating, has trouble breathing, has a seizure, or seems worse at any point. If you miss a dose, call your vet or us for what to do; don't double up on your own.

Getting GS-441524 from Pharmacy on the Park

We understand how urgent FIP is, and we prioritize FIP prescriptions. Your veterinary office can fax the prescription to 407-977-0079 or call 407-977-9779 with your cat's current weight, the dose and directions. We call you when we receive it, confirm the price, and let you know when it's ready. Pick up in Oviedo, or we ship to Florida, Maine and Colorado. When the dose changes with your cat's weight, your vet sends us a new prescription and we call you.

Common questions

Is FIP contagious to my other cats?

The feline coronavirus spreads between cats, mostly through litter boxes, but FIP itself develops inside an individual cat and isn't thought to spread the way a typical infection does. Ask your veterinarian about your other cats and good litter box hygiene.

Can my cat be cured?

Many cats treated with GS-441524 recover and go on to live normal lives, though not every cat responds. Your veterinarian is the best person to talk through your cat's outlook.

Why does the dose keep changing?

The dose is based on weight, and recovering cats often gain weight. That's a good sign. Your vet adjusts the prescription, and we fill the new strength.

This article is general information and not veterinary advice. Your veterinarian determines the diagnosis, the dose and how your cat is monitored. GS-441524 is not FDA-approved, and compounded medications are not commercially manufactured products.
